Cabbage is such a versatile vegetable, and this wintry take on a classic makes the most of its virtues

Cabbage will always be a top-tier vegetable in my eyes – it’s so versatile, from braising to roasting, from shredding it into a fritter to slowly cooking into a soup. I love it! This salad started life as a barbecue side dish, with the dressing made in advance and the wedges slowly charred over hot coals. If you’re a year-round barbecuer, then absolutely give this a go, but for everyone else, the oven-roasted version is just as excellent.

items.title: Brioche armchairs, butter sculptures and edible chandeliers: meet the new food artists
items.summary:
Culinary artists are turning fashion shows and design fairs into a feast for the eyes

A pretty Venetian chandelier featuring delicate pink flowers and cascading blue leaves hangs from a ceiling. A hazy, warm light radiates from its tulip bulbs. Suddenly, a woman reaches up and snaps off one of the flower stems, giggling as she begins to nibble it. Welcome to the weird and wonderful world of Laila Gohar. The Egyptian-born, New York-based artist is part of a new wave of culinary artists blurring the lines between sustenance and spectacle, and this troupe have quickly become a firm fixture at fashion parties and design fairs, turning dining into a phenomenon and delight.

Gohar describes the chandelier, made entirely from hand-spun sugar (including the silver chain that suspended it) as her “favourite thing she has done in recent history”. It joins a long list of extravagant yet still edible installations she has created, including lifesize armchairs made of brioche, an entire room constructed with Belgian chocolate and a four-metre-long mortadella that had to be lifted into the party’s venue using a crane.

items.title: A taste of Italy: Alessandro Giannatempo’s recipes for Amalfi-style ricotta and pear cake, and crocodile’s porridge
items.summary:
Sweet from top to toe: a creamy, southern Italian fruit and nut cake, and an almondy polenta porridge from the north

Although I grew up in Emilia-Romagna, my family history spans the Italian peninsula. Inspired by my mixed upbringing, these recipes reflect the flavours of both southern and northern Italy. The Amalfi-style ricotta and pear cake, as the name suggests, is a nod to the southern coast of Salerno. Fresh ricotta is whipped with lemony pears and sandwiched between layers of nutty hazelnut cake. The crocodile’s porridge, named after a traditional Italian beverage made with milk and pear juice, combines northern ingredients such as polenta and amaro for a very cosy stovetop-made dessert – or breakfast, if you ask me!

items.title: The best thing I ever ate? Lunch on the strait of Hormuz
items.summary:
The idea of any guest being hungry, or there not being enough food, is an unspeakable proposition for an Iranian host

When most people think of the strait of Hormuz, the warm, tropical waterway connecting the Persian Gulf and the Gulf of Oman, incredible food isn’t usually the first thing that comes to mind. But it should be, and I would know – it’s where I had one of my most memorable meals.

I was visiting Iran, traversing thousands of miles across the country with a local female photographer, mapping out regional specialities for my cookbook The Saffron Tales. Over the course of several months, we cooked and ate in people’s home kitchens, meeting a cross-section of society, from farmers and pharmacists to yoga teachers and restaurant owners, who all shared their favourite foods with us in places as diverse as the snowy mountains outside Tabriz, the rice paddies of the Caspian Sea, and the historic cities of Isfahan and Shiraz.

The Saffron Tales: Recipes and Stories from the Persian Kitchen by Yasmin Khan, published by Bloomsbury at £26. To order a copy for £23.40, go to guardianbookshop.com

items.title: Cassette, London WC2: ‘One of the greatest dishes I’ve eaten all year’ – restaurant review | Grace Dent on restaurants
items.summary:
A discombobulating brew of the seemingly casual with the deadly bloody serious

I booked my lunch table at Cassette, a new French restaurant in Covent Garden, central London, while watching a viral video of a blasé Parisian couple, mid-riot, sipping wine and smoking Gauloises near the Arc de Triomphe. Yes, fiery flames of mass anarchy, but also, yes, finishing one’s glass is important, too. The Brits keep opening Parisian-style restaurants as a quiet admission that these people are really bloody cool, and this new one from Mark Gurney and Matt Bushnell, the pair behind Peckham’s Levan (also very cool, incidentally), serves the likes of a coq au vin jaune pie with a chicken leg saluting from its crust, and panisse with chopped mussels and green tomato. There’s also pork chop with sauce Talleyrand, Maldon oysters with beurre blanc, and a cocktail called Jet Fuel that combines Get 27, the green mint liqueur that gives every Parisian a starry-eyed memory of their parents’ dinner parties, with calvados and coffee liqueur.

items.title: ‘Bland, faintly sugary and cardboardy’: the best (and worst) supermarket porridge oats, tasted and rated
items.summary:
Which get the day off to a satisfying start – and which make for a gruelling breakfast?

• The best supermarket natural yoghurts

In the winter of 2003-04, my girlfriend and I hosted a Scottish family at a chalet in Val d’Isère. Full of chef bravado, I promised the father that I’d make him the best bowl of breakfast porridge he’d ever had. He, of course, turned up his nose at my bowl of sweet dessert, which I’d laced with cream and sugar, and showed me how to make porridge with just water and salt instead. I’ve never looked back.

In my experience, most jumbo oats need twice as much water as the packet instructions suggest, as well as three times as long to cook and turn satisfyingly creamy. Regular and vigorous stirring is essential, too, as is the sea salt, which turns a bland bowl of pap into a naturally sweet, earthy and nutty porridge.

items.title: What 8 Cool Food People Outsource for Thanksgiving
items.summary:
This story was previously published as part of that series. Subscribe to Eater Today to see more of our editors’ boldest opinions about dining culture writ large. 

A few Novembers ago, I had a mild crash out over puff pastry. I was planning to meet my partner’s extended family for the first time over Thanksgiving, and volunteered to bring a holiday staple a few weeks prior (in what was one of the most helpful, albeit intimidating Excel sign-up sheets I’ve ever seen). What could be easier than apple pie? The ingredients for the recipe I found weren’t fussy, and it hardly called for fancy technical skills. Plus, I could make it ahead of time knowing that it would travel well. 

Then I remembered the puff pastry. For some reason, I attached a moral imperative to the idea of making the whole pie from scratch, and spent the next two weeks poring over puff pastry recipes that felt like casual guides to wizard-tier alchemy. I loved to cook, but I simply wasn’t a big baker. (I also didn’t own a food processor, unless you counted my Magic Bullet.) My mother eventually brought me down to Earth. “Just buy it,” she told me over the phone, undoubtedly rolling her eyes. “Everyone knows it’s a pain in the butt.” Even the Barefoot Contessa herself, she reminded me, famously avoids the time-consuming task ( “Nobody wants to make puff pastry!” ). 

Those words set me free. Once I realized that I could outsource my puff pastry, and the source of my Thanksgiving stress, I was finally able to relax and enjoy the holiday. Folks take pride in their Turkey Day dishes, as they should, but there’s…

items.title: The Thanksgiving food traditions we could all share
items.summary:
Warming pie, buttery mash and plenty of gravy are a perfect excuse to gather friends around the table during chilly November

• Sign up here for our weekly food newsletter, Feast

As a Brit, there are plenty of reasons for me not to embrace Thanksgiving, most of all because it isn’t actually a British holiday, and least of all because we already have quite enough occasions to eat ourselves silly between now and January. And yet, every November, as the days grow shorter and darker and colder, I find myself rather taken with the idea of hosting a seasonal dinner for friends. If Christmas is more formal and family-focused, then Thanksgiving feels like a prime opportunity to get pals around the table, eat until you need to undo your top trouser button, and take a moment to appreciate what you have. And if that means borrowing a few ideas from across the Atlantic – a warming spiced pumpkin pie, say, or a dish of fruity stuffing and a sharp cranberry sauce – well, there’s no reason we can’t make them our own.

items.title: Rachel Roddy’s recipe for pasta all’arrabbiata with red onion and plums | A kitchen in Rome
items.summary:
Much like tomato, the plum has a natural acidity and sweetness that works brilliantly in a delightfully jammy pasta sauce

Standing on platform 2 at Baker Street station a few weeks ago, a grey creature scuttled under the raised tracks. “You’re never more than six feet away from a rat in London,” I said to my Roman son. “It’s a mouse, Mum,” was his hardboiled reply to my rehashing of an urban myth. A myth that turns out to be inaccurate, according to Dr David Cowan, whose research on the subject resulted in estimates of anything from 10ft-164ft: in other words, while it’s impossible to know for sure, in certain areas you might be very close to a rat.

The same can be said about wild plum trees all over the world. While it’s impossible to know exactly, even in dense urban areas, you might be very close to a wild plum tree or, more correctly, a cultivated plum that has gone feral. Hedgerows, field margins, woodland edges, abandoned parks and wastelands are all places in which you might find yourself close to a plum tree; its branches decorated with fruit, some the size of marbles, others lozenges or eggs, and their spectrum of colour ranging from deep purple to powdery light blue, red, pink, gold and green.

items.title: Celebrating the Eater Awards Winners With a Party in NYC
items.summary:
A room full of winners | As Is Productions 

What a night. On Sunday, November 15, the winners of the 2026 Eater Awards, presented by Capital One, celebrated together at Nine Orchard in NYC. More than 200 chefs, restaurateurs, bartenders, and friends of Eater — many of whom traveled across the country to be there — partook in live portraiture, custom engraving, and, of course, plenty of food and drink.

Now in its 17th year, the Eater Awards recognize the year’s best new restaurants, bakeries, bars, dishes, and chefs in markets across the U.S.. More than 30 Eater staffers and contributors spent months traveling to 44 cities to weigh contenders on food, service, atmosphere, and the stories behind them. The prize? A tomato can trophy. And yes, they’re real.

The night started off strong with photos at the tomato can-wrapped step-and-repeat and a welcome shot of Zbiotics, before guests headed up to the roof of Nine Orchard for panoramic views and more fun. The party was filled with unique moments, from custom lighter engraving presented by Toast to live water color portraits presented by Capital One. Rounds of dishes inspired by the winning restaurants were passed. 

A champagne toast commemorated the resiliency of the hospitality industry. “Thank you for what you do, every single day, to bolster your team, your community, and the restaurant industry at large,” said Eater editor in chief Stephanie Wu.

items.title: The Best Little Gifts Your Holiday Party Host Will Actually Want
items.summary:
A good host is always thinking of others, whether it’s by making guests feel welcome, accommodating everyone’s diets, or setting an Instagram-worthy tablescape to make the night feel extra special. But the holiday season is an opportunity to flip the script and show the host you’re thinking of them, too. Bringing them a gift is the cardinal way to thank the host for all their thoughtful work. The only question remains: what to give?

For those who delight in trotting out their special dinnerware for guests, there’s a world of creative and whimsical gifts out there, even if it seems like they already have the entire CB2 catalog. And if that is the case, this just means you, as the gift-giver, can allow them to indulge in the things they typically would not. Take, for instance, some unique vintage shot glasses, intricately carved chopsticks, and pearl cocktail picks. Not only do these playful takes on essentials inspire joy, but they’re also sure to be conversation starters for future gatherings. And, as the bestower of the new treasured piece, you just might secure yourself the invite for the next one.

They can always use more serving utensils 

You can never have enough serving utensils if you love to host. That moment when you toss your pasta salad, plate everyone’s green beans, or dole out your main dish is an opportunity to flex some of your more decorative yet functional kitchen tools. This excerpt was originally published in Pre Shift, our newsletter for the hospitality industry, in an issue presented by Square. Subscribe for more first-person accounts, advice, and interviews .

This is not your average “gifts for foodies” round-up. We know that you’ve probably been given a few too many wine glasses and cookbooks. “As a professional, I don’t want to be gifted introductory-level items that will ultimately go unused,” says Storm Brunni, private dining director at Barolo Grill in Denver. That’s why, for our guide, we’ve consulted you, the hospitality pros, about what you actually would like to receive this year.

New shoes for service. “I’m getting all of my favorite people the new high-top kitchen shoes by Chuck Taylor in leather anti-slip. They’re cool enough to complete your streetwear look, functional enough to wear in the dining room, kitchen, or work, and comfy enough to wear as a commuter.” —Jonathon Sawyer, chef at Kindling in Chicago 

An industry-favorite hand cream . “Between constant handwashing, citrus, chiles, and hot pans, hospitality hands take a beating. Add a heated neck massager to use on the couch after a midnight close, and you’ve basically given someone a spa day.” —Antelmo Ambrosio, executive chef at Casa Oaxaca in New York City 

Something for the coffee nerds. “It’s definitely a splurge, but I buy myself the Onyx Coffee Advent Calendar every year.
